warmup.q: A flow emits yesterday's loaf, then calls the bakery inside withTimeout(50). Below it sits .catch { emit(crackers) }. The bakery takes 100 ms. What does the collector get?
options: Yesterday's loaf, then the timeout escapes, because catch never handles a CancellationException
Nothing at all: the timeout cancels the collector
Yesterday's loaf, and then the flow completes normally with nothing else
warmup.why: withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException inside the upstream while the collecting job is still running. To catch that is an upstream failure like any other, so the action runs and emits the crackers. What catch lets pass is the cancellation of the collecting job itself, and exceptions thrown below it.

opening:
Bread for dinner comes from the bakery round the corner, ordered by phone. It's a lovely bakery with a terrible phone. Sometimes the call drops halfway, and sometimes nobody picks up at all. So the cook has a routine. She rings again after a short pause, a longer pause each time, and if the corner bakery still can't help, she rings the backup bakery across town. Meanwhile plates can drop anywhere: in the kitchen, or at the table.

Kotlin flows have an operator for each part of that routine: catch for a dropped plate, retry for ringing again, timeout for giving up at a time limit, and onCompletion for the note about how it all ended. The easy trap is to believe that catch never sees a timeout, because a timeout is a kind of cancellation. It does see it, and that turns out to be useful.

In Flattening and combining, one failing inner flow took all the others down. In this lesson, we'll find which failures a catch hears, what a retry cooks again, what the note at the end says, and where a time limit goes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bakery that drops calls. catch is a net that hears only what falls from above it, timeouts included, and lets the caller's own cancellation through. A retry cooks the recipe again from the top, onCompletion leaves one note that can say "no more, thanks", and a timeout's position decides whether it limits one try or all of them.

Now search your own code for retry on a flow whose values change something, such as rows written to a database. Ask what happens when the same item arrives twice.

Next, we'll share one cooking session among many diners. What does a hot flow do when one diner is slow, and when its cook fails?

sections.h: A catch is a net under the upstream, and it checks who threw
sections.html:
Here is the bread course as a flow, a recipe card for values. The cook, the producer, cooks it only when a diner, the collector, calls collect, and each emit hands one value to the diner. The cook first sends out yesterday's loaf, then fetches a fresh one from the bakery inside withTimeout(50), which cancels the call if it takes longer than 50 ms. A catch below it, an operator (a helper on the way from the cook to the diner), sends out crackers if anything goes wrong. The bakery takes 100 ms today.

Most people expect the timeout to fly straight past the catch. The reasoning sounds solid: a timeout is a CancellationException, the exception a coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread) uses to say "stop, you've been called off", and catch doesn't handle cancellation. Run it, and then run a second version where the caller's own job, the handle that can cancel the collecting coroutine, is cancelled instead:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: onErrorResume handles what comes from above it; dispose() is a cancel signal
Flux.concat(Flux.just(oldLoaf), bakery.fresh().timeout(Duration.ofMillis(50)))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(crackers))
    .subscribe(diner::eat);               // case 2: the subscription is disposed meanwhile
Kotlin
flow { emit(oldLoaf); emit(withTimeout(50) { bakery.fresh() }) }   // the call takes 100 ms
    .catch { e -> emit(crackers) }
    .collect { diner.eat(it) }            // case 2: the caller calls job.cancel() meanwhile

Here is what the Try it prints for five ways the bread course can end. (An IOException is Java's usual exception for a failed read, write or call, such as a dropped phone line.)

How it ends The catch action runs The caller sees
the bakery call throws IOException yes nothing
the bakery call throws CancellationException yes nothing
withTimeout fires inside the bakery call yes, with TimeoutCancellationException nothing
the diner drops a plate no IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate
the caller's job is cancelled no JobCancellationException

The timeout was caught, and the cancelled job was not. To see why, remember lesson 2 of this track. An exception thrown by the collector, the diner, comes back out of emit and up into the cook's code, and the inspector refuses any emit after that. That rule is called exception transparency: an exception from downstream belongs to downstream. So when the upstream's collect throws, catch has to work out who threw. Build it by hand and the rule falls out:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same bookkeeping around a push-style source and a Consumer
static <T> void myCatch(Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream, Function<Throwable, T> action) {
    RuntimeException[] fromDownstream = {null};
    try {
        upstream.accept(v -> { try { downstream.accept(v); } catch (RuntimeException e) { fromDownstream[0] = e; throw e; } });
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        if (e == fromDownstream[0]) throw e;                                   // below the net
        if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw e;                   // our own task was cancelled
        downstream.accept(action.apply(e));                                    // an upstream failure
    }
}
Kotlin
fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow {
    var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null
    try {
        collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } }
    } catch (e: Throwable) {
        if (e === fromDownstream) throw e                                              // below the net
        if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // our job is cancelled
        action(e)                                                                      // an upstream failure
    }
}

Read it top to bottom. First it wraps the downstream emit and remembers anything that comes out of it. Then, when the whole collect fails, it asks two questions. Did this come from downstream? Rethrow it. Is it the cancellation of our own job? Rethrow that too. Everything else goes to your action.

The library's catch keeps the same books. Picture a net strung under the upstream, everything above catch in the chain, while the downstream is everything below it, the collector included. Anything that falls from above lands in the net, even a CancellationException that the upstream throws while the job is still running. The job's own cancellation passes through on purpose. And a plate the diner drops falls below the net, straight to the caller.

So catch ignores the cancellation of its collector, not every CancellationException. For a bakery call, that's usually what you want: a timeout becomes crackers. If it isn't, rethrow CancellationException in the action yourself.

The net is generous, but it only covers what hangs above it. To put the serving under its protection, move it into onEach above the catch and call collect() with no lambda, or launchIn(scope), which collects in a new coroutine of that scope (the owner of a group of coroutines, which cancels them all when it is cancelled). And a caught error still ends the upstream: flowOf(1, 2, 3).map { fails on 2 }.catch { emit(-1) } gives 1 and -1, and 3 is never made.

catch hears only what falls from above it. Put the work it should cover above it.

Check yourself: catch sits above map, and map throws. Who handles it? The net can send out crackers. Sometimes you'd rather ring the bakery again.

try.title: Five ways to end the bread course
steps: Open CatchNet.kt. For each of the five cases, predict whether the net catches it and what the caller sees.
Run it. Each case runs twice: once with the library's catch, once with myCatch from this section. Check that the two lines always agree.
In myCatch, delete the line that rethrows fromDownstream and run again. Which case changes, and what does the caller see now?
Run CatchNetJava, the onErrorResume twin. Find the case where moving the serving above the net changes the result.

code.title: CatchNet.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowCollector import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.io.IOException // catch, built by hand: remember what the downstream threw, and leave our own job's cancellation alone. private fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow { var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null try { collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } // 1. who threw? } } catch (e: Throwable) { if (e === fromDownstream) throw e // 2. not ours: below the net if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // 3. our job is cancelled action(e) // 4. an upstream failure } } private fun describe(e: Throwable?) = e?.let { "${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}" } ?: "nothing" // The bread course: yesterday's loaf goes out first, then a fresh one from the bakery. Five ways for it to end. private val cases: List<Pair<String, Flow<String>>> = listOf( "the bakery call throws IOException" to flow { emit("old loaf"); throw IOException("line dropped") }, "the bakery call throws CancellationException" to flow { emit("old loaf"); throw CancellationException("bakery gave up") }, "withTimeout inside the bakery call" to flow { emit("old loaf"); withTimeout(50) { delay(100) }; emit("fresh loaf") }, "the diner drops a plate" to flow { emit("old loaf"); emit("fresh loaf") }, "the caller's job is cancelled" to flow { emit("old loaf"); awaitCancellation() }, ) private fun run(label: String, net: String, f: Flow<String>) { var caught: Throwable? = null val netted = if (net == "catch") f.catch { caught = it; emit("crackers") } else f.myCatch { caught = it; emit("crackers") } val got = mutableListOf<String>() var callerSaw: Throwable? = null runBlocking { val job = launch { try { netted.collect { got += it; if (label.startsWith("the diner") && it == "old loaf") error("the diner dropped the plate") } } catch (e: Throwable) { callerSaw = e; if (e !is CancellationException) Unit else throw e } } if (label.startsWith("the caller")) { delay(10); job.cancel() } job.join() } println(" %-8s got %-22s net caught %-48s caller saw %s".format(net, got, describe(caught), describe(callerSaw))) } fun main() { for ((label, f) in cases) { println("== $label") run(label, "catch", f) run(label, "myCatch", f) } }

alt.title: CatchNetJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; // Closest Java equivalent of catch: Reactor's onErrorResume, which also handles only what comes from above it. public class CatchNetJava { static void run(String label, Flux<String> loaves, boolean serveAboveTheNet) { List<String> got = new ArrayList<>(); String[] caught = {"nothing"}; Flux<String> pipeline = serveAboveTheNet ? loaves.doOnNext(CatchNetJava::serve) : loaves; pipeline = pipeline.onErrorResume(e -> { caught[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage(); return Mono.just("crackers"); }); if (!serveAboveTheNet) pipeline = pipeline.doOnNext(CatchNetJava::serve); String callerSaw = "nothing"; try { pipeline.doOnNext(got::add).blockLast(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { callerSaw = e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage(); } System.out.printf("%-46s got %-24s net caught %-58s caller saw %s%n", label, got, caught[0], callerSaw); } static void serve(String loaf) { // the diner drops the second plate if (loaf.equals("fresh loaf")) throw new IllegalStateException("the diner dropped the plate"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("the bakery call fails with IOException", Flux.concat(Flux.just("old loaf"), Flux.error(new IOException("line dropped"))), false); run("the bakery is slow: timeout(50 ms) above the net", Flux.concat(Flux.just("old loaf"), Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn("fresh loaf")).timeout(Duration.ofMillis(50)), false); run("serving below the net", Flux.just("old loaf", "fresh loaf"), false); run("serving above the net (doOnNext first)", Flux.just("old loaf", "fresh loaf"), true); String[] caught = {"nothing"}; Disposable subscription = Flux.concat(Flux.just("old loaf"), Flux.<String>never()) .onErrorResume(e -> { caught[0] = e.toString(); return Mono.empty(); }) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.printf("%-46s doFinally %s, net caught %s%n", "the subscriber cancels", signal, caught[0])) .subscribe(); Thread.sleep(20); subscription.dispose(); } }

try.expect: The first three cases get [old loaf, crackers] and the caller sees nothing: the net caught an IOException, a CancellationException and a TimeoutCancellationException ("Timed out waiting for 50 ms"). The dropped plate and the job cancellation pass: the caller sees IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate and JobCancellationException. catch and myCatch agree on every line. Without the fromDownstream check, the dropped-plate case runs the action and emits again after the downstream failed, and the flow throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated. In Reactor, the dropped plate fails the stream when the serving sits below onErrorResume, and is handled when it sits above it.

video.title: catch is a net under the cook that asks who threw: an upstream timeout lands in it and becomes crackers, while the diner's dropped plate and the caller's own cancel go past; retry(3) cooks the recipe again from the top, and a backoff rings the bakery at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms

sections.h: A retry cooks the recipe again, from the top
sections.html:
The grocer's van is back with the delivery note from Context and threads: flour, eggs and butter, read line by line. On the first attempt the reader loses its connection after line 2, with an IOException. The pantry import wraps the note in retry(3). What does the pantry receive?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: retry re-subscribes, so a cold Flux replays from the top too
List<String> received = Flux.defer(grocer::note).retry(3).collectList().block();
// [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, butter]
Kotlin
val received = note.retry(3).toList()
// [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, butter]

Two lines went into the pantry twice. The flour doesn't mind, but the pantry book now lists it twice. retryWhen, the operator under retry, is a loop around the same books that catch keeps. When the upstream fails with an exception from above the net, it calls your predicate, a function that answers yes or no, with the cause and an attempt number. If the answer is yes, it collects the upstream again. A cold flow is a recipe card, and collecting it again cooks it again from the top. Values that were already emitted are emitted again.

The counting follows from the loop. retry(n) is retryWhen { cause, attempt -> attempt < n && predicate(cause) }, so retry(2) on a note that always fails collects it 3 times, and then the third exception comes out. retry(0) fails when you build the flow, with Expected positive amount of retries, but had 0. The default is Long.MAX_VALUE, which retries for ever. attempt is 0 on the first failure, and with retry(n, predicate) the predicate is no longer called once the attempts run out.

The cook's longer pause each time is a backoff, and in code it is a delay inside the predicate:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's backoff spec (jitter off, so the times are exact)
bakery.order("sourdough").retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)
        .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException));
Kotlin
bakery.order("sourdough").retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
    val retry = cause is IOException && attempt < 3
    if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt())        // 100, 200, 400 ms
    retry
}

Against a bakery that never answers, both ring at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms. Then they differ. Flow gives up by letting the original IOException out. Reactor wraps it in a RetryExhaustedException (Retries exhausted: 3/3, with the real error as its cause), and outside tests it adds jitter, a random spread on each wait so that many callers don't ring at the same moment (0.5 by default, from lesson 5 of the reactive track). Flow has no jitter, no cap and no exhaustion type. You write those yourself, which is what the lab does.

Like catch, a retry never fires for an exception the collector threw, or for the caller's own cancellation. It does fire for a TimeoutCancellationException from a timeout() above it, and the last section builds on that.

The replay is the part that hurts whenever each value changes something, such as a line in the pantry book. Every consumer after a retry must be idempotent: seeing the same item twice must leave the same result as seeing it once. Skip lines whose id you have seen (one set per collection), or make the source start where it stopped, from a bookmark that a retry can pass back.

A retry cooks the recipe again from the top. Make whatever comes after it safe to see an item twice.

Check yourself: retry(3) on a note that fails after its second line on every attempt. How many times does the collector see line 1? A retry hides failures well. A tally of how each order ended should hide nothing, and it's easy to get wrong.

retry(3)") var attempt = 0 val feed = flow { attempt++ log(" attempt $attempt starts") for (i in 1..3) { delay(10) if (attempt == 1 && i == 3) throw IOException("reader lost the connection") emit(listOf("flour", "eggs", "butter")[i - 1]) } } log("the pantry received ${feed.retry(3).toList()}") } runTest { println("== retry(2) on a note that always fails after two lines") var calls = 0 val r = flow { calls++; emit("flour"); emit("eggs"); throw IOException("dropped #$calls") } .retry(2) .catch { e -> log(" gave up: ${e.message}"); emit("PHONE THE GROCER") } .toList() log("collector saw $r after $calls collections") try { flow { emit(1) }.retry(0) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println(" retry(0): ${e.message}") } } runTest { println("== retryWhen with exponential backoff: 100, 200, 400 ms; IOException only") var n = 0 val result = flow { n++; log(" call $n to the bakery"); if (n <= 5) throw IOException("line dropped (call $n)"); emit("ok") } .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> val retry = cause is IOException && attempt < 3 log(" attempt=$attempt -> ${if (retry) "retry in ${100L shl attempt.toInt()} ms" else "give up"}") if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt()) retry } .catch { e -> log(" the original error comes out: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}"); emit("crackers") } .toList() log("result $result") } }

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.Exceptions; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's retry re-subscribes, so a cold Flux replays from the top too. public class RetryReplayJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== the delivery note: the reader loses the connection after line 2 on the first attempt; retry(3)"); AtomicInteger attempt = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<String> feed = Flux.defer(() -> { int n = attempt.incrementAndGet(); return n == 1 ? Flux.concat(Flux.just("flour", "eggs"), Flux.error(new IOException("reader lost the connection"))) : Flux.just("flour", "eggs", "butter"); }); System.out.println(" the pantry received " + feed.retry(3).collectList().block()); System.out.println("== Retry.backoff(3, 100 ms) with jitter off, on a call that always fails (real time)"); quiet = true; backoff(); // a silent first round loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; backoff(); } static void backoff() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<String> bakery = Flux.defer(() -> { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format(" call %d at about %d ms", calls.incrementAndGet(), Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); return Flux.error(new IOException("line dropped")); }); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { bakery.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)).blockLast(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (!quiet) System.out.println(" caller saw " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage() + "; isRetryExhausted=" + Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) + "; cause: " + e.getCause()); } } }

try.expect: The pantry receives [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, butter]. retry(2) collects 3 times: [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, flour, eggs, PHONE THE GROCER], and retry(0) is refused with "Expected positive amount of retries, but had 0". The backoff calls come at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, then the original IOException reaches the catch. With the predicate, an IOException is not retried, so you get [flour, eggs, PHONE THE GROCER] after 1 collection. Reactor replays the same five lines, rings at about 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, and ends with RetryExhaustedException: Retries exhausted: 3/3.

sections.h: The onCompletion note is written once, and its cause is not always a failure
sections.html:
The kitchen keeps a tally of bread orders: a tick for each one that went well, a cross for each one that failed. The orders go through first(), which takes the first value and stops. At the end of the evening, every order has a cross:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: doFinally reports a signal type instead of a cause
loaves(kind)
    .doFinally(signal -> { if (signal == SignalType.ON_COMPLETE) tally.ok(); else tally.failed(signal); })
    .next()
    .block();
Kotlin
loaves(kind)
    .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause == null) tally.ok() else tally.failed(cause) }
    .first()

onCompletion is a try/finally around the upstream, placed exactly where you wrote it. It runs once, when the flow ends, and leaves a note: its cause says what passed through that spot on the way out.

How the flow ended cause
it completed normally null
the upstream threw IOException: line dropped
the collector threw IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate
a map below threw, and a catch below that swallowed it IllegalStateException: map failed
above take(1) or first() AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed
below take(1) null
the collecting job was cancelled JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled

first() stops the upstream the way lesson 2 of this track described. It throws AbortFlowException, the signed "no more, thanks" note, out of the upstream's emit. That exception is a CancellationException, and every operator above first() sees it go by, so the tally counts a stopped order as a failed one. Below take(1) the flow simply ended, so the cause there is null.

So read the note in order. null means it went well. A CancellationException means it was called off or stopped early, which is not a failure. Anything else is a failure. In code, that is one more branch before the cross: cause is CancellationException -> tally.stopped().

onCompletion can emit, but only on success: flowOf("a", "b").onCompletion { if (it == null) emit("done") } gives a, b, done. After a failure, emit there throws the original cause again. Use catch to send out a replacement.

The terminal operators, the calls such as first() and single() that run a flow and return a result, fail in their own words, and they stop the upstream at different points. first() on an empty flow throws NoSuchElementException: Expected at least one element. single() throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty, or IllegalArgumentException: Flow has more than one element. On a three-element flow, first() pulls 1 element and single() pulls 2 before it fails. Reactor's single() says Source was a (constant) empty, and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item instead.

Check yourself: onCompletion sits below take(1), and the collector throws on the first element. What is cause? Every failure so far arrived quickly. The worst bakery is the one that never answers.

try.expect: null for success and below take(1). IOException: line dropped for the upstream failure, IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate for the collector failure, and IllegalStateException: map failed even though a catch below swallowed it. AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed above take(1) and above first(), and JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled for job.cancel(). single() pulls 2 elements and first() pulls 1. Reactor reports onComplete, onError, cancel above take(1) and onComplete below it.

sections.h: A timeout throws a cancellation, and its position sets what it limits
sections.html:
The corner bakery has stopped answering: each call now rings for 1,000 ms. The chain gives every call 300 ms, retries with backoff and then rings the backup bakery. When does the backup answer?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the Reactor chain from lesson 5 of the reactive track
bakery.order("sourdough")
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))
    .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0).filter(this::isTransient))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || isTransient(e), e -> backup.order("sourdough"));
Kotlin
bakery.order("sourdough")
    .timeout(300.milliseconds)            // per try; @FlowPreview
    .retryWithBackoff()                   // 3 retries: 100, 200, 400 ms
    .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(backup.order("sourdough")) }

Here isTransient is the lab's question "is this failure worth another try?": yes for a dropped line and for a timeout, no for anything else. The calls start at 0, 400, 900 and 1,600 ms, and each one is cut at +300. At 1,900 ms the corner bakery gives up with Timed out waiting for 300ms, and the backup answers at 1,930. Reactor's chain prints the same times on a real clock.

timeout(d) arrived in kotlinx.coroutines 1.7.0 and is still @FlowPreview in 1.11.0. It takes a Duration only. It runs the upstream in a producer coroutine and arms a timer only while it waits for the next upstream value. Time the downstream spends on a value doesn't count, but the wait for the first value does. Picture the kitchen's egg timer, wound each time the cook starts waiting for the bakery and paused while the diner eats. When it rings, it throws TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a CancellationException.

That one fact explains the rest of the chain. The timeout comes from above retryWhen while the job is still running, so retryWhen can retry it, but only if isTransient lists TimeoutCancellationException, because a timeout is not an IOException. Position sets the meaning. Above retryWhen, the timer limits each try. Below it, the timer limits the whole sequence, waits included: a budget. Add .timeout(1.seconds) after the retries, and the same bakery gets calls at 0, 400 and 900, the budget rings at 1,000, and the backup answers at 1,030.

The catch at the end filters on isTransient, so moon bread, which nobody bakes, reaches the caller as an IllegalArgumentException at 20 ms, with no retry and no call to the backup. When the backup fails too, the caller sees the backup's error. The corner bakery's error is not attached.

Above the retry, a timeout limits one try. Below it, a timeout limits them all.

The cancellation nature bites when the flow runs in the background. A timeout that nobody catches inside launch or launchIn just ends that coroutine as cancelled. The scope's CoroutineExceptionHandler, its last-resort handler for failures that nobody caught, never runs, and the parent scope keeps going, because handlers ignore CancellationException. Your bread refresher stops, and nobody hears the egg timer. Translate the timeout at the edge: .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) throw BakeryTimeout(e) else throw e }, and the handler gets BakeryTimeout with the timeout as its cause. Reactor's timeout signals java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException, an ordinary error, so the trap doesn't exist there.

Two notes for tests. Under runTest, withTimeout words its message differently ("Timed out after 50ms of virtual (kotlinx.coroutines.test) time..."), so assert on the exception's type, never its text. And TimeoutCancellationException has no public constructor, so produce one with a real timeout() under virtual time, as the lab does.

Check yourself: where does .timeout(1.seconds) go to limit each try instead of the whole sequence? Everything in this lesson acts on one collector and its own cold flow. When many diners share one cooking session, a failure behaves very differently.

try.title: Time a bakery that won't answer
steps: Open FlakyBakery.kt. Before you run it, write down when each of cases A to E ends, and how many calls each bakery gets.
Run it on virtual time and compare. Case E is case B with an overall timeout(1.seconds) after the retries.
Read the last block: the same timeout inside launchIn, first silent, then translated into BakeryTimeout.
Run FlakyBakeryJava, the Reactor version of case B, on a real clock.

code.title: FlakyBakery.kt
code.html: @file:OptIn(FlowPreview::class) package workbench.flows.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.FlowPreview import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.emitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.launchIn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.retryWhen import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.single import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.timeout import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.test.StandardTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestCoroutineScheduler import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import java.io.IOException import kotlin.time.Duration import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds @OptIn(kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private suspend fun now() = currentCoroutineContext()[TestCoroutineScheduler]!!.currentTime private suspend fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format(now(), msg)) /** script(n) says what call n does: a latency in ms, or an exception thrown after 20 ms. */ private class Bakery(val name: String, val script: (Int) -> Any) { var calls = 0 fun order(kind: String): Flow<String> = flow { val n = ++calls log(" $name call $n starts") when (val step = script(n)) { is Long -> { delay(step); emit("$kind from $name") } is Throwable -> { delay(20); throw step } } } } private fun transient(e: Throwable) = e is IOException || e is TimeoutCancellationException private fun <T> Flow<T>.backoff(max: Long = 3, first: Duration = 100.milliseconds): Flow<T> = retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (attempt >= max || !transient(cause)) return@retryWhen false val wait = first * (1L shl attempt.toInt()).toDouble() log(" retry ${attempt + 1} after ${cause::class.simpleName}, waiting $wait") delay(wait) true } private fun case(title: String, bakery: Bakery, backup: Bakery, budget: Duration? = null) = runTest { println("== $title") var f = bakery.order("sourdough").timeout(300.milliseconds).backoff() if (budget != null) f = f.timeout(budget) val loaf = f.catch { e -> if (!transient(e)) throw e log(" the corner bakery gave up (${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}); calling the backup") emitAll(backup.order("sourdough")) } val outcome = runCatching { loaf.single() }.fold({ "result: $it" }, { "caller saw ${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message}" }) log(" $outcome (corner calls ${bakery.calls}, backup calls ${backup.calls})") } class BakeryTimeout(cause: Throwable) : Exception("the bakery timed out", cause) fun main() { case("A: two dropped calls, then a 50 ms answer", Bakery("corner") { n -> if (n <= 2) IOException("line dropped") else 50L }, Bakery("backup") { 30L }) case("B: the corner bakery always takes 1000 ms", Bakery("corner") { 1_000L }, Bakery("backup") { 30L }) case("C: a bread nobody bakes is not transient", Bakery("corner") { IllegalArgumentException("nobody bakes moon bread") }, Bakery("backup") { 30L }) case("D: both bakeries closed", Bakery("corner") { IOException("corner bakery closed") }, Bakery("backup") { IOException("backup bakery closed") }) case("E: B again, with timeout(1s) as an overall budget", Bakery("corner") { 1_000L }, Bakery("backup") { 30L }, budget = 1.seconds) println("== a timeout that escapes launchIn is a cancellation: nobody hears it") runTest { val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> println(" handler got ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } val scope = CoroutineScope(Job() + handler + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) val silent = flow { delay(200); emit(1) }.timeout(50.milliseconds).launchIn(scope) silent.join() println(" silent: job cancelled=${silent.isCancelled}, scope active=${scope.isActive}") val loud = flow { delay(200); emit(1) }.timeout(50.milliseconds) .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) throw BakeryTimeout(e) else throw e } .launchIn(scope) loud.join() println(" loud: job cancelled=${loud.isCancelled}, scope active=${scope.isActive}") } }

alt.title: FlakyBakeryJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.Exceptions; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; // Closest Java equivalent of the flaky-bakery pattern: Reactor's timeout, retryWhen(Retry.backoff) and // onErrorResume. Case B: the corner bakery always takes 1000 ms. Real time, so expect a few ms of drift. public class FlakyBakeryJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; static final AtomicInteger cornerCalls = new AtomicInteger(); static void log(String msg) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format("%5d ms (about %4d) %s", ms, Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50, msg); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); } static Mono<String> corner() { return Mono.defer(() -> { log(" corner call " + cornerCalls.incrementAndGet() + " starts"); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1_000)).thenReturn("sourdough from corner"); }); } static Mono<String> backup() { return Mono.defer(() -> { log(" backup call starts"); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(30)).thenReturn("sourdough from backup"); }); } static boolean transientError(Throwable e) { return e instanceof IOException || e instanceof TimeoutException; } public static void main(String[] args) { quiet = true; run(); // a silent first round loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; run(); } static void run() { cornerCalls.set(0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); String loaf = corner() .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0).filter(FlakyBakeryJava::transientError)) .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || transientError(e), e -> { log(" the corner bakery gave up: " + e.getMessage() + " (cause: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ")"); return backup(); }) .block(); log(" result: " + loaf + " (corner calls " + cornerCalls.get() + ")"); } }

try.expect: A ends at 390 ms with a loaf from the corner bakery (3 calls). B: calls at 0, 400, 900 and 1,600, the corner bakery gives up at 1,900 with "Timed out waiting for 300ms", and the backup answers at 1,930. C: the caller sees IllegalArgumentException: nobody bakes moon bread at 20 ms, with no retry. D: the caller sees IOException: backup bakery closed at 800. E: the budget rings at 1,000 ("Timed out waiting for 1s") and the backup answers at 1,030. In the launchIn block, the silent version leaves the scope active and calls no handler; the loud version reaches the handler, and the scope is no longer active. Reactor's case B starts calls at about 0, 400, 900 and 1,600 ms and answers from the backup at about 1,950.

compare.title: One slow bakery call, as a Reactor chain and as a Flow chain

java.title: Reactor
java.html: Mono<Loaf> freshLoaf(String kind) { return Mono.defer(() -> bakery.order(kind)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // TimeoutException: an ordinary error .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // jitter 0.5 by default .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // overall budget .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || e instanceof TimeoutException, e -> backup.order(kind)); // exhausted: RetryExhaustedException }

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow
kotlin.html: @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) fun freshLoaf(kind: String): Flow<Loaf> = bakery.order(kind) .timeout(300.milliseconds) // TimeoutCancellationException: a cancellation .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> // no jitter, no cap unless you write them val retry = isTransient(cause) && attempt < 3 if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt()) retry } .timeout(1.seconds) // overall budget .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(backup.order(kind)) } // the original error

compare.note: The two chains have the same shape and, with jitter off, the same timeline. What differs is what the errors are. Reactor's timeout signals TimeoutException, an ordinary error, while Flow's throws TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, so you must list it in isTransient, and a timeout that escapes a launch ends that coroutine silently. Reactor wraps exhausted retries in RetryExhaustedException, while retryWhen lets the original exception out. Reactor's backoff has jitter, a cap and an exhaustion error built in, and in Flow you write the policy yourself. One thing Flow gives you for free: catch and retryWhen never act on the collecting job's own cancellation, so a caller that goes away stops the whole chain without a retry or a call to the backup.

worked.title: Order the bread, one decision at a time

steps.say: Give each call its own 300 ms and retry the failures worth retrying, with backoff. The timeout sits above the retry, so retryWhen sees each timeout and can retry it. List the timeout in isTransient, because it is not an IOException.
steps.code: fun isTransient(e: Throwable) = e is IOException || e is TimeoutCancellationException @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) val tries = bakery.order(kind) .timeout(300.milliseconds) // 1. per try .retryWithBackoff() // 2. 100, 200, 400 ms; the original error after that

lab.title: A flaky bakery: timeouts, backoff, a backup, and a note that replays
steps: Run the tests once. All 12 fail. Every timing in ErrorsTest is virtual, and each test name states the rule.
In Retries.kt, write isTransient, then retryWithBackoff with retryWhen. The wait before retry k is first * 2^k, capped at max.

In Bread.kt, write freshLoaf: timeout(300.milliseconds), then retryWithBackoff(), then a catch that rethrows failures that aren't transient and otherwise emits all of the backup's flow. Predict the four bakery tests' times before you run them.
Read the cancellation test. Work out why your freshLoaf passes it without any extra code.
Fix eachLineOnce so a retry can't deliver a line twice, and so a second collection still delivers every line.
hints: retryWhen's lambda gets (cause, attempt), and attempt starts at 0. Return false to let the original exception out, and delay before returning true.
Duration times Double works: first * (1L shl attempt.toInt()).toDouble(), then minOf(..., max).
timeout is @FlowPreview in 1.11.0, so freshLoaf needs @OptIn(FlowPreview::class). Without it you only get a warning.
For eachLineOnce, create the set of seen ids inside a flow { } builder, so each collection gets a fresh one. A set created outside it is shared by every collector.

drill.title: Write catch from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> with flow { }. It must rethrow what the downstream threw, rethrow the cancellation of its own job, and hand everything else to action. Then say which of these reaches action: an upstream withTimeout firing, the collector throwing, job.cancel().

answer.html: fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow { var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null try { collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } // 1. remember what the collector threw } } catch (e: Throwable) { if (e === fromDownstream) throw e // 2. below the net if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // 3. our job action(e) // 4. from upstream } } // Only the upstream withTimeout reaches action: it is a CancellationException, but our job is still running.

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a push-style source and a Consumer, with the same three checks static <T> void myCatch(Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream, Function<Throwable, T> action) { RuntimeException[] fromDownstream = {null}; try { upstream.accept(v -> { try { downstream.accept(v); } catch (RuntimeException e) { fromDownstream[0] = e; throw e; } // 1. remember what the consumer threw }); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (e == fromDownstream[0]) throw e; // 2. below the net if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw e; // 3. our own task was cancelled downstream.accept(action.apply(e)); // 4. from upstream } }

recap: A downstream exception comes out of emit. catch remembers it and rethrows it, and it rethrows its own job's cancellation. Everything else from upstream reaches the action, a CancellationException or TimeoutCancellationException included.
Work in collect { } is below the net. Put it in onEach above catch, then call collect() or launchIn.

retry(n) means n retries and n + 1 collections, and each one replays the upstream from the top. Whatever comes after a retry must be idempotent. retryWhen's attempt starts at 0, a delay in it is the backoff, and the original exception comes out at the end.
onCompletion's cause is null on success, the exception on failure, JobCancellationException on cancel, and AbortFlowException above take or first. Read a CancellationException as stopped, not failed.
timeout() throws TimeoutCancellationException, a cancellation. Above retryWhen it limits each try, below it is a budget, and uncaught in a launch it ends silently, so translate it.
The limit: all of this acts on one collector and its own cold flow. When many collectors share one upstream, a failure in it never reaches them, which is the next lesson's surprise.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why catch { emit(crackers) } turns a bakery timeout into crackers, but does nothing when the diner leaves and the caller is cancelled. They thought catch never sees a CancellationException. Explain it with the net picture, and say what you'd add if the flow ran in a background launchIn job.
explain.answer: catch is a net under the upstream. It wraps the downstream's emit and remembers anything the collector throws, which it rethrows, and it rethrows the cancellation of its own collecting job. Everything else that falls from above lands in the net. A withTimeout or timeout() inside the bakery call throws TimeoutCancellationException while our job is still running, so to catch it's just an upstream failure, and the action sends out crackers. When the diner leaves, the caller's job is cancelled. That cancellation is the job's own, so the net lets it pass and no crackers are sent, which is what we want. In a background launchIn job I'd add a translation. If both bakeries time out, the TimeoutCancellationException would escape the launch as a plain cancellation, no exception handler would run and the refresher would stop silently. So I'd convert it in a catch into a BakeryTimeout exception of my own, which the scope's handler logs.

deeper.html:
When both sides fail, the upstream wins. If the collector throws IllegalStateException("collector failed") and the builder's finally then throws IOException("close() failed"), the caller sees the IOException, with the collector's exception in suppressed, and a catch above does not run its action. The Flow KDoc calls this "a semantic equivalent of throwing from finally block", and notes that the exception-handling operators still treat the downstream exception as the root cause.

A failed backup forgets the first bakery. flow { throw IOException("corner bakery closed") }.catch { emitAll(flow { throw IOException("backup bakery closed") }) } gives the caller IOException: backup bakery closed with no cause and nothing suppressed. If you want both in the logs, attach the first one yourself with addSuppressed before you emit from the backup.

Don't retry from inside catch with emitAll(sameFlow). The catch KDoc points to retryWhen, which retries "without introducing ever-growing stack of suspending calls".

withTimeoutOrNull(250) { flow.toList() } returns null and loses the values that arrived before the deadline. Collect into a list you own (collect { partial += it }) if you need them. Inside runBlocking with a CoroutineName("bread-refresher"), the withTimeout message names the coroutine: Coroutine "bread-refresher" timed out waiting for 50 ms.

The exact boundary of timeout(100.milliseconds) depends on how the scheduler orders events at the same instant: under virtual time a 100 ms gap did not time out and a 101 ms gap did. Don't build logic on the equality case.

onEmpty { emit(default) } is the counterpart for a flow that completes without a value: a dish with no sauce of its own gets the house sauce, and a dish with one gets its own.

sources.title: operators/Errors.kt at tag 1.11.0 (catch, retry and retryWhen)
